decks.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry - Part 1: Points in space and the distance formula
goals: Place a point in space from its coordinates and name its octant
Find the feet of perpendiculars and the distances of a point from the axes, the planes and the origin
Use the distance formula, leaving answers as simplified surds
Decide whether three points are collinear and name a triangle from its sides

slides.heading: Three-dimensional geometry, Part 1
slides.body_md: Axes, planes, octants, feet of perpendiculars and the distance formula.

nodes.label: Feet and distances from axes and planes

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: coordinates, axes, planes and octants, then feet of perpendiculars and distances from axes and planes, then the distance formula, then triangle types and collinear points.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four steps.

slides.narration: Welcome to three-dimensional geometry. In this first part we place points in space using three axes, name the octant of a point, and find the feet of perpendiculars. Then we derive the distance formula and use it to test whether three points lie on a line and to name a triangle. Every coordinate in this chapter was computed and checked twice.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Locate a point from $(x, y, z)$ and name its **octant**
Find **feet** and **distances** from axes and planes
Test **collinearity** and name **triangles** from squared sides

rows: Place a point and name its octant
Find feet and distances from axes and planes
Find the distance between two points

visual.alt: Table of goals for Part 1: octants, feet and distances, the distance formula, and collinearity and triangle types.
visual.caption: What Part 1 covers.

slides.narration: By the end of this part you will locate a point from its three coordinates and name its octant. You will find feet of perpendiculars and distances from the axes and the planes. You will use the distance formula and leave answers as simplified surds. And you will test whether three points are collinear and decide what kind of triangle they form.

slides.heading: Axes and coordinate planes
slides.body_md: Three mutually perpendicular lines through the **origin** $O$ are the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes. Each pair of axes spans a **coordinate plane**: the $xy$-, $yz$- and $zx$-planes.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the x, y and z axes meeting at the origin O at right angles. Three square patches mark the xy-plane between the x and y axes, the yz-plane between the y and z axes, and the zx-plane between the z and x axes.
visual.caption: The axes and the three coordinate planes (oblique sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Three lines at right angles to each other meet at the origin. They are the x axis, the y axis and the z axis. Each pair of axes spans a flat surface called a coordinate plane. The x and y axes span the x y plane, the y and z axes span the y z plane, and the z and x axes span the z x plane. The three planes divide space into eight regions.

slides.heading: Coordinates of a point
slides.body_md: A point $P$ has coordinates $(x, y, z)$: the distances from the $yz$-, $zx$- and $xy$-planes, with signs. To reach $P(2, 5, 3)$ go $2$ along the $x$-axis, $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis and $3$ parallel to the $z$-axis; the box has diagonal $OP$.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the axes with a rectangular box whose corner at the origin O is opposite the corner P at 2, 5, 3. The edges lie along the axes: 2 units along x, 5 along y and 3 along z. The corner N at 2, 5, 0 below P is marked.
visual.caption: P(2, 5, 3): 2 along x, 5 along y, 3 along z (oblique sketch, not to scale).

math: P(x, y, z): \quad x = \text{distance from the } yz\text{-plane}
slides.narration: A point is described by three numbers. The x coordinate is its signed distance from the y z plane, the y coordinate is its signed distance from the z x plane, and the z coordinate is its signed distance from the x y plane. In the picture the point is reached by going two along x, five along y and three along z. These three steps are the edges of a box whose opposite corner is the origin.

slides.heading: Points on axes and in planes
slides.body_md: A zero coordinate puts a point in a plane; two zero coordinates put it on an axis; all three give the origin.

visual.alt: Table: points on the three axes and in the three coordinate planes, with the coordinates that are zero and one example of each.
visual.caption: Which coordinates are zero.

slides.narration: Zero coordinates tell you where a point sits. If exactly one coordinate is zero the point lies in a coordinate plane. If two coordinates are zero it lies on an axis, and the one that is not zero says how far along. If all three are zero it is the origin. The table shows the condition for each position with an example.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: where does each point lie?
bullets: Count the zero coordinates in each point
Two zeros: an axis; one zero: a plane; none: an octant
$(-5, -1, -2)$ has three negative signs, so octant VII

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: each of six points with its zero coordinates and its position (the y-axis, the zx-plane, the xy-plane, the yz-plane, octant VII, the z-axis).
visual.caption: Position from the zero coordinates.

slides.narration: For each point, count the zero coordinates. The first point has two zeros, so it is on the y axis. The second has only y equal to zero, so it is in the z x plane. The third has z zero, so it is in the x y plane. The fourth has x zero, so it is in the y z plane. The fifth has no zero and three negative signs, so it is in octant seven. The last has two zeros, so it is on the z axis.

slides.heading: Quick check: an axis
slides.body_md: A point lies on the $y$-axis. Which coordinates must be zero?
slides.narration: A point on the y axis can move only in the y direction. So the other two coordinates must both be zero. Decide which one is missing from the sentence.

slides.heading: The eight octants
slides.body_md: The three planes cut space into **octants**. Octant I has all coordinates positive; II to IV are above the $xy$-plane going round; V to VIII are the same pattern below. A point with a zero coordinate is on a boundary, not in an octant.

visual.alt: Table of the eight octants with the sign of x, y and z in each, and an example point: octant I has plus, plus, plus; II minus, plus, plus; III minus, minus, plus; IV plus, minus, plus; V to VIII repeat these with z negative.
visual.caption: Octants I to IV have z positive; octants V to VIII are their copies below the xy-plane.

slides.narration: The three coordinate planes cut space into eight octants. Octant one has all three coordinates positive. Octants two, three and four go round above the x y plane, and octants five to eight repeat the same pattern below it. The table gives the signs and an example for each octant. A point with a zero coordinate is on a boundary, so it belongs to no octant.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming octants
slides.body_md: Name the octant of $(4, -7, -1)$ and of $(-2, -6, 8)$, and of a point with $x < 0$, $y > 0$, $z < 0$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 2: the point 4, minus 7, minus 1 lies in octant VIII, the point minus 2, minus 6, 8 in octant III, and a point with x negative, y positive, z negative in octant VI.
visual.caption: Reading the octant from the signs.

slides.narration: Read the signs of the three coordinates, in order. The point four, minus seven, minus one has signs plus, minus, minus, which is octant eight. The point minus two, minus six, eight has signs minus, minus, plus, which is octant three. A point with x negative, y positive and z negative has signs minus, plus, minus, which is octant six.

slides.heading: Quick check: boundary points
slides.body_md: A point has $z = 0$ and positive $x$ and $y$. Is it in octant I?
slides.narration: Remember what a zero coordinate means. Then decide whether the point can belong to an octant.

slides.heading: Feet of perpendiculars
slides.body_md: The foot of the perpendicular from $P(x, y, z)$ to a **plane** replaces the coordinate that is zero in that plane by $0$. The foot on an **axis** keeps only the coordinate along that axis.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the axes with a point P at 2, 4, 3 above the xy-plane. A vertical segment drops from P to its foot F at 2, 4, 0 on the xy-plane, and a dashed segment joins P to M at 2, 0, 0, the foot of the perpendicular on the x-axis.
visual.caption: F is the foot of P on the xy-plane (PF = 3); M is the foot on the x-axis (PM = 5) (oblique sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: To find the foot of the perpendicular on a coordinate plane, replace the coordinate that is zero in that plane by zero. To find the foot on an axis, keep the coordinate along the axis and make the other two zero. In the picture the point two, four, three drops to the x y plane at two, four, zero, and to the x axis at two, zero, zero.

slides.heading: Distances from planes, axes and the origin
slides.body_md: The distance from a plane is the absolute value of one coordinate. The distance from an axis uses the other two coordinates. All of these follow from the distance formula.

visual.alt: Table of distances of the point minus 2, 6, 9 from the three planes (2, 6 and 9), the three axes (3 root 13, root 85 and 2 root 10) and the origin (11), with the general formula for each.
visual.caption: Distances of a point from planes, axes and the origin.

slides.narration: The distance of a point from a coordinate plane is the absolute value of one coordinate. The distance from an axis is the square root of the sum of squares of the other two coordinates. The distance from the origin uses all three. The table works these out for the point minus two, six, nine, giving eleven for the origin and surds for the axes.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: feet and distances
slides.body_md: For $Q(5, -3, -4)$ find the foot on the $zx$-plane, the foot on the $z$-axis, and the distance from the $x$-axis.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3 about the point 5, minus 3, minus 4: its foot on the zx-plane is 5, 0, minus 4; its foot on the z-axis is 0, 0, minus 4; its distance from the x-axis is 5.
visual.caption: Feet and a distance for $Q(5, -3, -4)$.

slides.narration: The z x plane has y equal to zero, so the foot is five, zero, minus four. The foot on the z axis keeps only z, so it is zero, zero, minus four. The distance from the x axis uses the other two coordinates, minus three and minus four. The square root of nine plus sixteen is five.

slides.heading: The distance formula
slides.body_md: Walk from $P$ to $Q$ along the edges of a box: the right triangle in a horizontal plane gives $PR^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2$, and a second right angle at $R$ gives the result.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of a path from P at 1, 1, 1 along the x direction by 3, then along the y direction by 4 to R at 4, 5, 1, then up by 2 to Q at 4, 5, 3. The dashed segment PR lies in a plane parallel to the xy-plane and has length 5; the segment PQ is the required distance.
visual.caption: PR² = 3² + 4² = 25 and PQ² = PR² + RQ² = 25 + 2² = 29 (oblique sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: To find the distance between two points, walk between them along the edges of a box. First the horizontal path of three and four makes a right triangle with hypotenuse five. Then the vertical rise of two makes another right angle. So the square of the distance is nine plus sixteen plus four. In general, add the squares of the three coordinate differences and take the square root.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a distance with a surd

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4: for A at minus 2, 5, 1 and B at 4, minus 1, minus 3 the coordinate differences are 6, minus 6 and minus 4, the squares add to 88, and the distance is 2 root 22.
visual.caption: AB for $A(-2, 5, 1)$ and $B(4, -1, -3)$.

slides.narration: Subtract the coordinates one at a time. The differences are six, minus six and minus four. Square them and add: thirty six plus thirty six plus sixteen is eighty eight. The distance is the square root of eighty eight. Since eighty eight is four times twenty two, we simplify it to two times the square root of twenty two.

slides.heading: Quick check: distance from the origin
slides.body_md: Use the distance formula with the origin as one point.
slides.narration: The origin has all coordinates zero, so the differences are just the coordinates of the point. Square them, add them and take the square root.

slides.heading: Naming a triangle from its sides
slides.body_md: Find the three squared sides first. Compare them: equal squares give equal sides, and two squares adding to the third give a right angle by the converse of Pythagoras.

rows: two squared sides add up to the third
two equal, and their sum equals the third
all three different and no such sum

visual.alt: Table of triangle tests by squared side lengths: equilateral has all three equal, isosceles exactly two equal, right-angled has two squared sides adding to the third.
visual.caption: Compare squared sides first; take roots last.

slides.narration: To name a triangle, find the three squared side lengths first and compare them. If all three are equal the triangle is equilateral. If exactly two are equal it is isosceles. If two of them add up to the third, the triangle is right angled. Work with squares until the very end, because they avoid surds.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a right-angled triangle
slides.body_md: Show that $A(1, 3, 0)$, $B(1, -3, 2)$, $C(-4, 3, 0)$ form a right-angled triangle.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5: the triangle with vertices A at 1, 3, 0, B at 1, minus 3, 2 and C at minus 4, 3, 0 has squared sides 40, 65 and 25, and 40 plus 25 equals 65, so the right angle is at A.
visual.caption: Right angle at $A$.

slides.narration: Find the three squared sides. A B squared is zero plus thirty six plus four, which is forty. B C squared is twenty five plus thirty six plus four, which is sixty five. C A squared is twenty five. Now forty plus twenty five equals sixty five, which is B C squared. So the right angle is at A, opposite the longest side.

slides.heading: Collinear points
slides.body_md: Three points are collinear when the longest of the three distances equals the sum of the other two. In a projection on the $xy$-plane, collinear points stay on one line.

visual.alt: Projection on the xy-plane of three points A, B and C that lie on one straight line in space; the projections A prime at minus 2, 3, B prime at 1, 1 and C prime at 7, minus 3 lie on one straight line.
visual.caption: Projection on the xy-plane: collinear points in space project to collinear points.

slides.narration: Three points lie on one straight line when the longest of the three distances equals the sum of the other two. Otherwise they form a triangle, because in any triangle the longest side is shorter than the sum of the other two. The picture shows the projection on the x y plane of three collinear points: their shadows also lie on one line.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: three points on a line?
slides.body_md: Test $A(-2, 3, 1)$, $B(1, 1, 5)$, $C(7, -3, 13)$ for collinearity.
bullets: So $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$

visual.alt: Table for worked example 6: for A at minus 2, 3, 1, B at 1, 1, 5 and C at 7, minus 3, 13 the distances are root 29, 2 root 29 and 3 root 29, and the first two add to the third, so the points are collinear.
visual.caption: The longest distance equals the sum of the other two.

slides.narration: Work out the squared distances: A B squared is twenty nine, B C squared is one hundred and sixteen, and A C squared is two hundred and sixty one. Taking roots, they are root twenty nine, twice root twenty nine and three times root twenty nine. The first two add up to the third, so the points are collinear, and B is between A and C.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Zero coordinates: one gives a plane, two give an axis
The signs of $(x, y, z)$ give the octant
Compare squared sides to name a triangle or test collinearity

rows: signs of $(x, y, z)$ fix the octant; a zero coordinate means a plane or axis
zero the coordinates; $\sqrt{y^2 + z^2}$ from the $x$-axis
compare squared sides; collinear when the longest is the sum of the other two

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: octants, feet and distances, the distance formula, and tests with squared sides.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up. Zero coordinates put a point in a plane or on an axis, and the signs of the coordinates give the octant. Feet of perpendiculars come from zeroing coordinates. Distances from the axes use two coordinates. The distance formula adds the squares of the three differences. And squared sides tell you the type of triangle and whether three points lie on a line.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Subtract coordinates in the same order for all three differences
Square, add, then take the root; simplify the surd
Compare squared sides before taking roots
Never place a point with a zero coordinate in an octant

rows: Square the differences and add before taking the root
Leaving a perfect square inside the root
Name the octant from the signs
Putting a point with a zero coordinate in an octant

visual.alt: Table of exam tips for Part 1: square then add the differences, simplify surds, use squared distances for equidistance, and name octants only from non-zero signs.
visual.caption: Marks in Part 1 come from clear steps.

slides.narration: In the examination, subtract the coordinates in the same order for all three differences, then square and add. Take the root at the end and simplify the surd. When naming a triangle, compare squared sides first. And remember that a point with a zero coordinate belongs to a plane or an axis, never to an octant.

decks.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry - Part 2: Quadrilaterals, loci and the section formula
goals: Classify a quadrilateral from distances and the mid-points of its diagonals
Find a point equidistant from given points, and write the equation of a plane or a sphere as a locus
Use the mid-point and section formulas, internal and external
Find where a coordinate plane cuts a segment, a centroid, and a missing vertex of a parallelogram

slides.heading: Three-dimensional geometry, Part 2
slides.body_md: Quadrilaterals, loci, the section formula and centroids.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: quadrilaterals and equidistant points, simple loci, the mid-point and section formulas, the ratio in which a coordinate plane divides a segment, and then collinearity, centroids and missing vertices of parallelograms.
visual.caption: Part 2 in five steps.

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. We begin by using distances to classify quadrilaterals and to find points that are equally far from two others, which leads to simple loci. Then we divide a segment in a given ratio, internally and externally, find where a coordinate plane cuts it, and finish with centroids and the missing vertex of a parallelogram.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Classify a **quadrilateral** from sides and diagonals
Describe a **locus** as a plane or a sphere
Use the **section formula** internally and externally

rows: Divide a segment internally or externally
Find where a plane cuts a segment
Test collinearity and find a missing vertex
common ratio for all three coordinates

visual.alt: Table of goals for Part 2: quadrilaterals, loci, the mid-point formula, internal and external division, where a coordinate plane cuts a segment, collinearity and missing vertices, and centroids.
visual.caption: What Part 2 covers.

slides.narration: By the end of this part you will classify a quadrilateral from its sides and diagonals, and describe a simple locus as a plane or a sphere. You will use the section formula for internal and external division, and find where a coordinate plane cuts a segment. You will also find centroids and the fourth vertex of a parallelogram.

slides.heading: Quadrilaterals from distances
slides.body_md: A common mid-point of the two diagonals makes $ABCD$ a parallelogram. Then equal adjacent sides give a rhombus and equal diagonals a rectangle. Equal sides alone do not guarantee a plane figure in space.

rows: opposite sides equal, or the diagonals have the same mid-point
a parallelogram with all four sides equal

visual.alt: Table of tests for quadrilaterals: parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle and square, using side lengths, diagonal lengths and the mid-points of the diagonals.
visual.caption: Sides, diagonals and mid-points settle the type.

slides.narration: To classify a quadrilateral, first check whether the diagonals share a mid-point. If they do, it is a parallelogram. Then equal adjacent sides make it a rhombus, and equal diagonals make it a rectangle. Both together make a square. In space four equal sides do not guarantee a flat figure, so always check the mid-points of the diagonals first.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: an equidistant point
slides.body_md: Find the point on the $y$-axis that is equally far from $A(3, -1, 2)$ and $B(-1, 5, 6)$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 7: the point P at 0, s, 0 on the y-axis equidistant from A at 3, minus 1, 2 and B at minus 1, 5, 6 satisfies s squared plus 2s plus 14 equals s squared minus 10s plus 62, so s is 4 and each distance is root 38.
visual.caption: Equidistant point on the $y$-axis.

slides.narration: A point of the y axis has the form zero, s, zero. Write the squared distances to the two given points and set them equal. The squares of s cancel, leaving twelve s equals forty eight. So s is four, and both distances are the square root of thirty eight. Working with squared distances avoids roots until the end.

slides.heading: A locus: the plane equidistant from two points
slides.body_md: The points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ satisfy $PA^2 = PB^2$. The squared terms cancel, so the condition is linear: a **plane** through the mid-point, perpendicular to $AB$.

visual.alt: Cross-section by the xy-plane: the points A at minus 2, 1 and B at 4, 3 lie in the plane; the line y equals 5 minus 3x is where the plane equidistant from A and B cuts the xy-plane, and it passes through the midpoint M at 1, 2.
visual.caption: Cross-section by the xy-plane of the plane equidistant from $A$ and $B$.

slides.narration: The set of points equally far from two given points satisfies P A squared equals P B squared. When you expand both sides, the squared terms cancel and a linear equation remains. So the locus is a plane, through the mid-point of the segment and at right angles to it. The picture shows its cross-section by the x y plane: a line through the mid-point.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: the set of points at a fixed distance
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the set of points $P$ at distance $7$ from $C(-3, 0, 4)$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 8: the points P at distance 7 from C at minus 3, 0, 4 satisfy x plus 3 all squared plus y squared plus z minus 4 all squared equals 49, which expands to x squared plus y squared plus z squared plus 6x minus 8z minus 24 equals 0.
visual.caption: The set of points 7 units from $(-3, 0, 4)$.

slides.narration: A point at a fixed distance from a fixed centre lies on a sphere. Square the distance formula: x plus three all squared, plus y squared, plus z minus four all squared, equals forty nine. Expanding gives x squared plus y squared plus z squared plus six x minus eight z minus twenty four equals zero. We only derive the equation here, and we do not go further into spheres.

slides.heading: The mid-point formula
slides.body_md: The mid-point of $A(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ averages each coordinate.

visual.alt: Projection on the xy-plane of the segment from A at 2, minus 3, 4 to B at 8, 5, minus 2: the projected points A prime at 2, minus 3 and B prime at 8, 5, with the projection of the midpoint M at 5, 1 halfway between them.
visual.caption: Projection on the xy-plane: the mid-point projects to the mid-point of the projections.

slides.narration: The mid-point of a segment averages each coordinate separately. Add the two x coordinates and halve, then do the same for y and for z. The picture shows the projection on the x y plane of a segment: the mid-point projects to the mid-point of the projections, which is why the averages work coordinate by coordinate.

slides.heading: The section formula: internal division
slides.body_md: If $P$ divides $AB$ internally with $AP : PB = m : n$, each coordinate is divided in the same ratio.

visual.alt: Table: dividing the segment from A at minus 4, 2, 5 to B at 6, minus 8, 0 in the ratio 2 to 3 divides each coordinate in the same ratio and gives the point 0, minus 2, 3.
visual.caption: Each coordinate is divided in the same ratio $m : n$.

math: P = \left(\dfrac{m x_2 + n x_1}{m + n}, \dfrac{m y_2 + n y_1}{m + n}, \dfrac{m z_2 + n z_1}{m + n}\right)
slides.narration: When a point divides a segment internally in the ratio m to n, every coordinate is divided in that same ratio. The formula takes m times the second coordinate plus n times the first, over m plus n. Notice the crossing: m goes with the second point. The table divides a segment in the ratio two to three, coordinate by coordinate.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: internal division
slides.body_md: $P$ divides $A(-5, 3, 8)$ to $B(7, -9, -4)$ with $AP : PB = 1 : 3$. Find $P$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1 of Part 2: A at minus 5, 3, 8 and B at 7, minus 9, minus 4 with AP to PB equal to 1 to 3 give P at minus 2, 0, 5, which lies in the zx-plane.
visual.caption: Internal division $1 : 3$.

slides.narration: Here m is one and n is three, so each coordinate has denominator four. For x, one times seven plus three times minus five, over four, is minus two. For y, one times minus nine plus three times three, over four, is zero. For z, one times minus four plus three times eight, over four, is five. The point has y equal to zero, so it lies in the z x plane.

slides.heading: Quick check: a mid-point coordinate
slides.body_md: Average the two $x$-coordinates.
slides.narration: Add the two x coordinates, then halve the sum.

slides.heading: External division
slides.body_md: If $P$ lies on line $AB$ outside the segment with $AP : PB = m : n$, use the same formula with $n$ replaced by $-n$. The denominator is $m - n$, and $m \ne n$.

visual.alt: Projection on the xy-plane of the line through A at 3, minus 2, 5 and B at 5, 2, 1. The point P at 9, 10, minus 7 that divides AB externally in the ratio 3 to 2 lies beyond B on the same line, so its projection P prime at 9, 10 is beyond B prime at 5, 2.
visual.caption: Projection on the xy-plane: an external point lies on the line beyond $B$.

math: P = \left(\dfrac{m x_2 - n x_1}{m - n}, \dfrac{m y_2 - n y_1}{m - n}, \dfrac{m z_2 - n z_1}{m - n}\right)
slides.narration: For external division the point lies on the line through the two points, but outside the segment. The formula is the same with n replaced by minus n, so the denominator is m minus n. The two parts must differ, because external division in the ratio one to one does not exist. In the picture, the external point lies beyond the second point on the same line.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: external division
slides.body_md: Find $P$ dividing $A(2, -1, 3)$ and $B(-4, 5, -3)$ externally in the ratio $5 : 3$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 2 of Part 2: A at 2, minus 1, 3 and B at minus 4, 5, minus 3 divided externally in the ratio 5 to 3 give P at minus 13, 14, minus 12.
visual.caption: External division $5 : 3$.

slides.narration: The ratio is five to three, so the denominator is five minus three, which is two. For x, five times minus four minus three times two, over two, is minus thirteen. For y, five times five minus three times minus one, over two, is fourteen. For z, five times minus three minus three times three, over two, is minus twelve.

slides.heading: Where a coordinate plane cuts a segment
slides.body_md: On the plane where coordinate $k$ is zero, $AP : PB = -a_k : b_k$. A positive ratio means internal division; a negative ratio means external, and the segment does not reach the plane.

visual.alt: Table of where the segment from A at 4, minus 2, 6 to B at minus 2, 5, 9 meets the three coordinate planes: the yz-plane internally in 2 to 1, the zx-plane internally in 2 to 5 and the xy-plane externally in 2 to 3, at 16, minus 16, 0.
visual.caption: Ratio $-a_k : b_k$; the sign says internal or external.

slides.narration: A coordinate plane is where one coordinate is zero. Put that coordinate into the section formula and solve for the ratio: it comes out as minus a over b, where a and b are the coordinates of the two end points. If the ratio is positive the plane cuts the segment itself. If it is negative the plane meets only the extended line, so the division is external.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: where the zx-plane cuts
slides.body_md: Find the ratio and the point where the $zx$-plane cuts $A(3, -8, 2)$ to $B(-1, 4, 6)$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3 of Part 2: the zx-plane divides the segment from 3, minus 8, 2 to minus 1, 4, 6 internally in the ratio 2 to 1, at the point one third, 0, fourteen thirds.
visual.caption: Where the $zx$-plane cuts $AB$.

slides.narration: On the z x plane y is zero, so the ratio is minus the first y over the second y. That is eight to four, which is two to one. Both parts are positive, so the plane cuts the segment itself. The section formula with two and one then gives one third, zero, fourteen thirds.

slides.heading: Quick check: a plane cut
slides.body_md: Use $-y_1 : y_2$ for the $zx$-plane.
slides.narration: On the z x plane the y coordinate is zero. Use minus the first y coordinate to the second y coordinate, and write the ratio in lowest terms.

slides.heading: Collinearity by the section formula
slides.body_md: $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear if one common ratio $\lambda$ makes all three coordinates fit. Find it from one coordinate, then check the other two.

rows: find the ratio $\lambda$ from one coordinate, then check the other two
the three differences are in the same proportion

visual.alt: Table of three ways to test whether three points are collinear: distances, the section formula with a common ratio, and proportional coordinate differences.
visual.caption: Three ways to test collinearity.

slides.narration: To test collinearity with the section formula, suppose the third point divides the join of the first two in some ratio. Find that ratio from one coordinate, then check that the other two coordinates give the same ratio. If they do, the points are collinear. If not, they are not. The table compares this with the distance method and with proportional differences.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a common ratio
slides.body_md: Test $A(1, -2, 3)$, $B(4, 1, 9)$, $C(7, 4, 15)$ for collinearity.
bullets: Check $z$: $\dfrac{3 + 15}{2} = 9$, so $B$ is the mid-point of $AC$

rows: $B(4, 1, 9)$ is the mid-point of $AC$, so $A$, $B$, $C$ are collinear

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4 of Part 2: for A at 1, minus 2, 3, B at 4, 1, 9 and C at 7, 4, 15 the x-coordinate gives the ratio 1 to 1 and the y and z coordinates confirm it, so B is the midpoint of AC and the points are collinear.
visual.caption: Collinearity by the section formula.

slides.narration: Suppose B divides A C in the ratio m to n. The x coordinate gives four equals seven m plus n over m plus n, so m equals n, and the ratio is one to one. Now check y: the average of minus two and four is one, which matches B. Check z: the average of three and fifteen is nine, which also matches. So B is the mid-point of A C, and the three points are collinear.

slides.heading: The centroid of a triangle
slides.body_md: The centroid $G$ is the average of the three vertices, and it divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ from the vertex.

visual.alt: Projection on the xy-plane of the triangle with vertices A at 3, 7, 5, B at minus 4, minus 2, 8 and C at 7, minus 2, minus 4, with the median from A to the midpoint D of BC. The centroid G at 2, 1, 3 projects to G prime at 2, 1 on that median, two thirds of the way from A prime to D prime.
visual.caption: Projection on the xy-plane of a triangle, its median $AD$ and the centroid $G$.

math: G = \left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3}, \dfrac{z_1 + z_2 + z_3}{3}\right)
slides.narration: The centroid of a triangle is the average of its three vertices. It lies on every median, two thirds of the way from the vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side. In the picture, the projections of the vertices form a triangle, the median from A runs to the mid-point D of the opposite side, and the centroid G sits on it.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the third vertex from the centroid
slides.body_md: $A(2, -4, 6)$, $B(-5, 1, 3)$ and the centroid $G(1, 2, -1)$ are given. Find $C$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5 of Part 2: with A at 2, minus 4, 6, B at minus 5, 1, 3 and centroid G at 1, 2, minus 1, the third vertex C is at 6, 9, minus 12.
visual.caption: The third vertex from the centroid.

slides.narration: The centroid is the average of the vertices, so the sum of each coordinate of the three vertices is three times the centroid coordinate. For x, three times one is three, minus two minus minus five, gives six. For y, six plus four minus one is nine. For z, minus three minus six minus three is minus twelve. So C is six, nine, minus twelve.

slides.heading: The centroid of a tetrahedron
slides.body_md: A tetrahedron has four vertices. Its centroid is the average of all four, and it divides the line from a vertex to the centroid of the opposite face in the ratio $3 : 1$.

visual.alt: Table: the centroid of a triangle is the average of three vertices and the centroid of a tetrahedron is the average of four; for the tetrahedron with vertices 0, 0, 0; 8, 0, 0; 0, 12, 0 and 0, 0, 16 it is 2, 3, 4.
visual.caption: Centroid = average of the vertices.

slides.narration: A tetrahedron has four corner points. Its centroid is the average of all four vertices. It lies on the line from each vertex to the centroid of the opposite face, three quarters of the way from the vertex. The table compares the triangle and the tetrahedron, and works one example with a corner at the origin.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tetrahedron centroid
slides.body_md: Average the four vertices coordinate by coordinate.
slides.narration: Add the four x coordinates and divide by four. Do the same for y and z, and compare with the given point.

slides.heading: A missing vertex of a parallelogram
slides.body_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. For $ABCD$ in order, equating the mid-points of $AC$ and $BD$ gives $D = A + C - B$.

visual.alt: Projection on the xy-plane of the parallelogram ABCD with A at minus 3, minus 2, 1, B at 2, minus 1, 4, C at 5, 3, 2 and the missing vertex D at 0, 2, minus 1, with both diagonals. They cross at the projection of their common midpoint M at 1, 1 over 2, 3 over 2.
visual.caption: Projection on the xy-plane of a parallelogram and its diagonals; they meet at the common mid-point.

slides.narration: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so they share a mid-point. For a parallelogram A B C D with vertices in order, the mid-point of A C equals the mid-point of B D. That gives D equals A plus C minus B. The picture shows the projection on the x y plane, with both diagonals crossing at the common mid-point.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: finding the fourth vertex
slides.body_md: Find $D$ for the parallelogram $ABCD$ with $A(-3, -2, 1)$, $B(2, -1, 4)$, $C(5, 3, 2)$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 6 of Part 2: for the parallelogram ABCD with A at minus 3, minus 2, 1, B at 2, minus 1, 4 and C at 5, 3, 2 the diagonals share the midpoint 1, one half, three halves, which gives D at 0, 2, minus 1.
visual.caption: Missing vertex from the equal mid-points of the diagonals.

slides.narration: The mid-point of A C is one, one half, three halves. The mid-point of B D must be the same, so two plus x equals two, minus one plus y equals one, and four plus z equals three. Solving gives x equal to zero, y equal to two and z equal to minus one. So D is zero, two, minus one.

$PA^2 = PB^2$ gives a plane; $PC^2 = r^2$ gives a sphere
Internal: $\dfrac{m x_2 + n x_1}{m + n}$; external: $\dfrac{m x_2 - n x_1}{m - n}$

sections.heading: 1. Axes, planes and coordinates
sections.body_md:
Three mutually perpendicular lines through the origin $O$ are the **coordinate axes**; each pair spans a **coordinate plane** ($xy$, $yz$, $zx$). A point $P(x, y, z)$ is reached by going $x$ along the $x$-axis, $y$ parallel to the $y$-axis and $z$ parallel to the $z$-axis: $x$, $y$, $z$ are the signed distances from the $yz$-, $zx$- and $xy$-planes.

A point with exactly one zero coordinate lies in a coordinate plane (for example $z = 0$ gives the $xy$-plane); two zero coordinates put it on an axis; all three give the origin.

key_terms.definition_md: The plane spanned by two axes; the $xy$-plane is $z = 0$, the $yz$-plane is $x = 0$, the $zx$-plane is $y = 0$.
The point $(0, 0, 0)$ where the three axes meet.

formulas.latex: xy\text{-plane: } z = 0, \quad yz\text{-plane: } x = 0, \quad zx\text{-plane: } y = 0
formulas.label: Coordinate planes

visuals.caption: Which coordinates are zero.

sections.heading: 2. Octants
sections.body_md:
The three planes divide space into eight **octants**. Octant I has $(+, +, +)$; octants II, III, IV are the other three $xy$-quadrants above the $xy$-plane, taken $(-, +)$, $(-, -)$, $(+, -)$; octants V to VIII repeat that order with $z < 0$.

A point belongs to an octant only if all three coordinates are non-zero. A point with a zero coordinate lies on a plane or an axis, which is a boundary between octants.

key_terms.definition_md: One of the eight regions into which the coordinate planes cut space, fixed by the signs of $x$, $y$, $z$.

visual.alt: Table of the eight octants with the sign of x, y and z in each, and an example point: octant I has plus, plus, plus; II minus, plus, plus; III minus, minus, plus; IV plus, minus, plus; V to VIII repeat these with z negative.

visuals.caption: Reading the octant from the signs.

sections.heading: 3. Feet of perpendiculars and distances
sections.body_md:
The foot of the perpendicular from $P(x, y, z)$ on a coordinate plane replaces the coordinate that is zero in that plane by $0$ (for the $yz$-plane, $(0, y, z)$). The foot on an axis keeps the coordinate along that axis (on the $x$-axis, $(x, 0, 0)$).

The distance of $P$ from the $yz$-, $zx$-, $xy$-planes is $\lvert x \rvert$, $\lvert y \rvert$, $\lvert z \rvert$; from the $x$-, $y$-, $z$-axes it is $\sqrt{y^2 + z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2 + z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$; from the origin $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The point where the perpendicular from $P$ meets a plane or an axis.

visual.caption: F is the foot of P on the xy-plane (PF = 3); M is the foot on the x-axis (PM = 5) (oblique sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 4. The distance formula
sections.body_md:
The distance between $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ is $PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$. Subtract in the same order, square, add, and then take the root; simplify any surd ($\sqrt{88} = 2\sqrt{22}$).

When only equality of distances matters, compare **squared** distances and avoid roots altogether.

key_terms.definition_md: The sum of the squares of the three coordinate differences, under a square root.

visual.caption: PR² = 3² + 4² = 25 and PQ² = PR² + RQ² = 25 + 2² = 29 (oblique sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 5. Collinearity, triangles and quadrilaterals
sections.body_md:
Three points are **collinear** when the longest of their three mutual distances equals the sum of the other two. A triangle is equilateral (three equal squared sides), isosceles (two equal) or right-angled (two squared sides add up to the third).

For a quadrilateral $ABCD$ in space, first test whether the diagonals have the same mid-point (a parallelogram). Equal adjacent sides then give a rhombus and equal diagonals a rectangle; both together give a square.

key_terms.definition_md: Lying on one straight line; the longest distance is the sum of the other two.
A parallelogram with all four sides equal.

rows: two squared sides add up to the third
two equal, and their sum equals the third
all three different and no such sum

visuals.caption: The longest distance equals the sum of the other two.

rows: opposite sides equal, or the diagonals have the same mid-point

sections.heading: 6. Equidistant points and simple loci
sections.body_md:
A point $(0, s, 0)$ (or $(s, 0, 0)$, $(0, 0, s)$) equidistant from $A$ and $B$ is found by equating $PA^2$ and $PB^2$; the terms in $s^2$ cancel and a linear equation remains.

In general $PA^2 = PB^2$ gives a **plane** through the mid-point, perpendicular to $AB$, and the points at a fixed distance $r$ from $C(a, b, c)$ satisfy $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = r^2$, a **sphere**. Only the equations are needed; expand them for the general form.

key_terms.definition_md: The set of all points satisfying a given condition.
The points at a fixed distance $r$ from a fixed point: $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = r^2$.

sections.heading: 7. Section formula, centroid and missing vertices
sections.body_md:
The mid-point of $AB$ averages each coordinate. If $AP : PB = m : n$, the internal point is $\dfrac{m x_2 + n x_1}{m + n}$ (and similarly for $y$, $z$); the external point is $\dfrac{m x_2 - n x_1}{m - n}$ with $m \ne n$. A coordinate plane cuts $AB$ in the ratio $-a_k : b_k$; a negative ratio means external division.

The centroid of a triangle is the average of its three vertices (dividing each median $2 : 1$); the centroid of a tetrahedron is the average of four (dividing the line to the opposite face centroid $3 : 1$). Collinearity can be tested with one common ratio; for a parallelogram $ABCD$ in order, $D = A + C - B$.

The average of the vertices; the common point of the medians of a triangle.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Octant, foot or distance from an axis (1-2 marks):* the signs or the zeroed coordinates, then the answer.
- *Distance between two points (2 marks):* the three differences squared and added, then the simplified root.
- *Collinearity or triangle type (3 marks):* the three squared sides or distances, the comparison, and the conclusion.
- *Equidistant point (2-3 marks):* $PA^2 = PB^2$ with the unknown, the cancellation, and the point.
- *Section formula (2-3 marks):* the ratio as $AP : PB$, the formula with $m$ and $n$ in the correct places, and each coordinate.
- *Plane cutting a segment (2-3 marks):* the zero coordinate, the ratio $-a_k : b_k$, internal or external, and the point.
- *Long questions (5 marks, in parts):* the feet or mid-points first, then the distances or ratio, then the conclusion, with a check.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the differences before squaring, or forgetting the square root.
- Putting a point with a zero coordinate into an octant.
- Swapping $m$ and $n$ in the section formula.
- Using $m + n$ instead of $m - n$ for an external point, or calling every plane cut internal.
- Checking only one coordinate when testing collinearity.
- Leaving $\sqrt{88}$ instead of $2\sqrt{22}$.
- Finding $D$ as $A + B - C$ for a parallelogram $ABCD$ in order.

questions.stem_md: A point $(a, b, c)$ lies in octant VI. Then
questions.solution_md: The octants run I to IV above the $xy$-plane with the $xy$-quadrants $(+, +)$, $(-, +)$, $(-, -)$, $(+, -)$, and V to VIII below it in the same order. questions.stem_md: The foot of the perpendicular drawn from $P(-4, 9, -2)$ to the $yz$-plane is

questions.solution_md: The nearest point of the $x$-axis is $(-6, 0, 0)$, so the distance is $\sqrt{8^2 + (-10)^2} = \sqrt{164} = 2\sqrt{41}$. The value $10$ is the distance from the $z$-axis, $2\sqrt{34}$ from the $y$-axis, and $10\sqrt{2}$ from the origin.

questions.stem_md: A point in octant VI is $3$ units from the $yz$-plane, $5$ units from the $zx$-plane and $2$ units from the $xy$-plane. Its coordinates are
questions.solution_md: The distances from the $yz$-, $zx$- and $xy$-planes are $\lvert x \rvert$, $\lvert y \rvert$, $\lvert z \rvert$, so the magnitudes are $3$, $5$, $2$. questions.stem_md: The points $A(3, -4, 2)$, $B(3, 3, 1)$, $C(-4, 2, 1)$ and $D(-4, -5, 2)$ are taken in order. Show that $ABCD$ is a rhombus but not a square.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ have mid-points $\left(\dfrac{3 - 4}{2}, \dfrac{-4 + 2}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 1}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, -1, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3 - 4}{2}, \dfrac{3 - 5}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 2}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, -1, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$, which are equal, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. $AB^2 = 0 + 49 + 1 = 50$ and $BC^2 = 49 + 1 + 0 = 50$, so adjacent sides are equal and it is a rhombus. Its diagonals are $AC^2 = 49 + 36 + 1 = 86$ and $BD^2 = 49 + 64 + 1 = 114$, which are different, so it is not a square.

questions.solution_md: A common mid-point of the diagonals gives a parallelogram; equal sides then give a rhombus; equal diagonals would make it a square.

questions.stem_md: A point $P(x, y, z)$ moves so that $PA^2 - PB^2 = 20$, where $A$ is $(2, -1, 3)$ and $B$ is $(-4, 3, 1)$. Show that $P$ stays on a plane and find its equation.

answer.model_answer_md: $PA^2 = (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 + (z - 3)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4x + 2y - 6z + 14$ and $PB^2 = (x + 4)^2 + (y - 3)^2 + (z - 1)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 8x - 6y - 2z + 26$. Subtracting, $PA^2 - PB^2 = -12x + 8y - 4z - 12 = 20$. The squared terms cancel, so the condition is linear: $-12x + 8y - 4z = 32$, that is $3x - 2y + z = -8$, which is a plane.

questions.solution_md: Expand both squared distances; the $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ terms cancel and leave a linear equation.

marking_scheme.step: The squared terms cancel, leaving a linear equation

questions.stem_md: The $xy$-plane meets the line through $A(1, -4, 3)$ and $B(7, 2, 9)$ at a point $P$. Find the ratio $AP : PB$, say whether $P$ lies between $A$ and $B$, and find the coordinates of $P$.

answer.model_answer_md: On the $xy$-plane $z = 0$, so $AP : PB = -z_1 : z_2 = -3 : 9 = -1 : 3$. The ratio is negative, so $P$ divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $1 : 3$ and does not lie between $A$ and $B$ (both points are above the plane). Then $P = \left(\dfrac{1(7) - 3(1)}{1 - 3}, \dfrac{1(2) - 3(-4)}{1 - 3}, \dfrac{1(9) - 3(3)}{1 - 3}\right) = (-2, -7, 0)$.

questions.solution_md: Use $z = 0$ to get the ratio, read its sign, then apply the external formula.

questions.stem_md: Three consecutive vertices of a parallelogram $PQRS$ are $P(-1, 4, 2)$, $Q(3, -2, 5)$ and $R(6, 1, -3)$. Find the fourth vertex $S$ and verify that the diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ bisect each other.

answer.model_answer_md: The diagonals bisect each other, so the mid-point of $PR$ equals the mid-point of $QS$. Mid-point of $PR$: $\left(\dfrac{-1 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{2 - 3}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{5}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$. With $S = (x, y, z)$: $\dfrac{3 + x}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, $\dfrac{-2 + y}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, $\dfrac{5 + z}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $S = (2, 7, -6)$. Check: the mid-point of $QS$ is $\left(\dfrac{5}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

questions.solution_md: Equate the mid-points of the two diagonals, then substitute $S$ back.

questions.stem_md: The point $P(4, y, z)$ lies on the straight line through $A(2, -1, 4)$ and $B(8, 5, -2)$. Find $y$ and $z$, and the ratio $AP : PB$.

answer.model_answer_md: Let $P$ divide $AB$ in the ratio $m : n$. Then $4 = \dfrac{8m + 2n}{m + n}$, so $4m + 4n = 8m + 2n$ and $2n = 4m$, giving $m : n = 1 : 2$. Then $y = \dfrac{1(5) + 2(-1)}{3} = 1$ and $z = \dfrac{1(-2) + 2(4)}{3} = 2$. So $P = (4, 1, 2)$ and $AP : PB = 1 : 2$.

questions.solution_md: The $x$-coordinate gives the ratio; the same ratio then fixes $y$ and $z$.

questions.stem_md: A tetrahedron has vertices $A(6, -2, 4)$, $B(-2, 6, 0)$, $C(4, 2, -6)$ and $D(0, -2, 2)$. Find its centroid $G$, find the centroid $F$ of the face $BCD$, and show that $G$ divides $AF$ in the ratio $3 : 1$ measured from $A$.

answer.model_answer_md: The centroid of the tetrahedron is the average of the four vertices: $G = \left(\dfrac{6 - 2 + 4 + 0}{4}, \dfrac{-2 + 6 + 2 - 2}{4}, \dfrac{4 + 0 - 6 + 2}{4}\right) = (2, 1, 0)$. The centroid of face $BCD$ is $F = \left(\dfrac{-2 + 4 + 0}{3}, \dfrac{6 + 2 - 2}{3}, \dfrac{0 - 6 + 2}{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}, 2, -\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$. The point dividing $AF$ in the ratio $3 : 1$ is $\left(\dfrac{3(2/3) + 1(6)}{4}, \dfrac{3(2) + 1(-2)}{4}, \dfrac{3(-4/3) + 1(4)}{4}\right) = (2, 1, 0) = G$.

questions.solution_md: Average four vertices for $G$, three for $F$, then use the internal section formula with $3 : 1$.

questions.stem_md:
A rectangular box has its faces parallel to the coordinate planes. Two opposite corners of the box are $A(-1, 2, -3)$ and $G(4, 6, 1)$. Find

(a) the coordinates of all eight corners, [2]

(b) the length of the diagonal $AG$, [1]

(c) the coordinates of the centre of the box, [1]

(d) the distance of the centre from the $xy$-plane. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The corners take every combination of $x \in \{-1, 4\}$, $y \in \{2, 6\}$, $z \in \{-3, 1\}$. On the face $z = -3$: $(-1, 2, -3)$, $(4, 2, -3)$, $(4, 6, -3)$, $(-1, 6, -3)$. On the face $z = 1$: $(-1, 2, 1)$, $(4, 2, 1)$, $(4, 6, 1)$, $(-1, 6, 1)$.

(b) $AG = \sqrt{(4 + 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2 + (1 + 3)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 16 + 16} = \sqrt{57}$.

(c) The centre is the mid-point of $AG$: $\left(\dfrac{-1 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{-3 + 1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 4, -1\right)$.

(d) The distance from the $xy$-plane is $\lvert z \rvert = \lvert -1 \rvert = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Corners come from the two values of each coordinate; the centre is the mid-point of a space diagonal.

questions.stem_md:
The points $A(-3, 4, 3)$, $B(0, -2, 3)$, $C(4, 0, -1)$ and $D(1, 6, -1)$ are taken in order. Find

(a) the lengths of the four sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$, [2]

(b) the lengths and the mid-points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, [2]

(c) the name of the quadrilateral $ABCD$, with a reason. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB^2 = 9 + 36 + 0 = 45$, so $AB = 3\sqrt{5}$; $BC^2 = 16 + 4 + 16 = 36$, so $BC = 6$; $CD^2 = 9 + 36 + 0 = 45$, so $CD = 3\sqrt{5}$; $DA^2 = 16 + 4 + 16 = 36$, so $DA = 6$.

(b) $AC^2 = 49 + 16 + 16 = 81$ and $BD^2 = 1 + 64 + 16 = 81$, so both diagonals have length $9$. The mid-point of $AC$ is $\left(\dfrac{-3 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 0}{2}, \dfrac{3 - 1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 2, 1\right)$ and the mid-point of $BD$ is $\left(\dfrac{0 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{3 - 1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 2, 1\right)$.

(c) The diagonals have the same mid-point, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram; they are equal in length, so it is a rectangle. It is not a square, because the adjacent sides $3\sqrt{5}$ and $6$ are different.

questions.solution_md: Compare the sides in pairs, then the diagonals; a common mid-point gives a parallelogram and equal diagonals make it a rectangle.

marking_scheme.step: Rectangle, not a square, with the reason

questions.stem_md:
The vertices of a triangle are $A(-1, 2, 4)$, $B(5, -4, 0)$ and $C(-1, -3, 5)$. Find

(a) the squares of the lengths of its three sides, [2]

(b) which angle of the triangle is a right angle, with a reason, [1]

(c) the mid-point $M$ of the longest side, and show that $MA = MB = MC$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB^2 = 36 + 36 + 16 = 88$, $BC^2 = 36 + 1 + 25 = 62$, $CA^2 = 0 + 25 + 1 = 26$.

(b) $BC^2 + CA^2 = 62 + 26 = 88 = AB^2$, so the angle at $C$ is a right angle and $AB$ is the hypotenuse.

(c) The longest side is $AB$, with mid-point $M = \left(\dfrac{-1 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{2 - 4}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 0}{2}\right) = (2, -1, 2)$. Then $MA^2 = 9 + 9 + 4 = 22$, $MB^2 = 9 + 9 + 4 = 22$ and $MC^2 = 9 + 4 + 9 = 22$, so $MA = MB = MC = \sqrt{22}$.

questions.solution_md: The longest squared side is the sum of the other two if the triangle is right-angled; the mid-point of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices.

questions.stem_md:
The points $A(-3, 5, 2)$ and $B(9, -7, 14)$ are given. Find

(a) the point $P$ that divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $AP : PB = 1 : 3$, [1]

(b) the point $R$ that divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $AR : RB = 3 : 1$, [2]

(c) the ratio in which the $xy$-plane divides $AB$, and the point where it meets the line $AB$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $P = \left(\dfrac{1(9) + 3(-3)}{4}, \dfrac{1(-7) + 3(5)}{4}, \dfrac{1(14) + 3(2)}{4}\right) = (0, 2, 5)$.

(b) For external division, $R = \left(\dfrac{3(9) - 1(-3)}{3 - 1}, \dfrac{3(-7) - 1(5)}{3 - 1}, \dfrac{3(14) - 1(2)}{3 - 1}\right) = (15, -13, 20)$.

(c) On the $xy$-plane $z = 0$, so $AP : PB = -z_1 : z_2 = -2 : 14 = -1 : 7$. The ratio is negative (both $A$ and $B$ lie above the plane), so the division is external in the ratio $1 : 7$. The point is $\left(\dfrac{1(9) - 7(-3)}{1 - 7}, \dfrac{1(-7) - 7(5)}{1 - 7}, \dfrac{1(14) - 7(2)}{1 - 7}\right) = (-5, 7, 0)$.

questions.solution_md: Internal division uses $m x_2 + n x_1$ over $m + n$; external division uses $m x_2 - n x_1$ over $m - n$; a coordinate plane gives the ratio $-a_k : b_k$.

questions.stem_md:
A triangle has vertices $A(5, -7, 9)$, $B(-3, 4, 1)$ and $C(1, 6, 5)$. Find

(a) the mid-point $D$ of $BC$, [1]

(b) the point $G$ on $AD$ with $AG : GD = 2 : 1$, [2]

(c) the centroid of the triangle, and say how it compares with $G$, [1]

(d) the length $AG$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $D = \left(\dfrac{-3 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{1 + 5}{2}\right) = (-1, 5, 3)$.

(b) $G = \left(\dfrac{2(-1) + 1(5)}{3}, \dfrac{2(5) + 1(-7)}{3}, \dfrac{2(3) + 1(9)}{3}\right) = (1, 1, 5)$.

(c) The centroid is $\left(\dfrac{5 - 3 + 1}{3}, \dfrac{-7 + 4 + 6}{3}, \dfrac{9 + 1 + 5}{3}\right) = (1, 1, 5)$, the same point as $G$: the centroid divides each median in the ratio $2 : 1$ from the vertex.

(d) $AG = \sqrt{(1 - 5)^2 + (1 + 7)^2 + (5 - 9)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 64 + 16} = \sqrt{96} = 4\sqrt{6}$.

questions.solution_md: Use the mid-point, then the internal section formula with $2 : 1$, then compare with the average of the vertices.

questions.stem_md:
$P(2, 1, -3)$, $Q(6, -1, 2)$ and $R(3, 5, 1)$ are three vertices of a parallelogram, but the order of the vertices is not stated. Find

(a) the three possible positions of the fourth vertex, [3]

(b) the centroid of triangle $PQR$ and the centroid of the triangle formed by the three positions found in (a), and show that they coincide. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The fourth vertex is opposite one of the three given vertices, and the diagonals bisect each other. If it is opposite $P$: $X = Q + R - P = (6 + 3 - 2, -1 + 5 - 1, 2 + 1 + 3) = (7, 3, 6)$. If it is opposite $Q$: $Y = P + R - Q = (2 + 3 - 6, 1 + 5 + 1, -3 + 1 - 2) = (-1, 7, -4)$. If it is opposite $R$: $Z = P + Q - R = (2 + 6 - 3, 1 - 1 - 5, -3 + 2 - 1) = (5, -5, -2)$.

(b) The centroid of $PQR$ is $\left(\dfrac{2 + 6 + 3}{3}, \dfrac{1 - 1 + 5}{3}, \dfrac{-3 + 2 + 1}{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{11}{3}, \dfrac{5}{3}, 0\right)$. The centroid of $XYZ$ is $\left(\dfrac{7 - 1 + 5}{3}, \dfrac{3 + 7 - 5}{3}, \dfrac{6 - 4 - 2}{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{11}{3}, \dfrac{5}{3}, 0\right)$. The two centroids coincide.

questions.solution_md: Use $A + C = B + D$ for each choice of the opposite pair, then average each triple of vertices.

marking_scheme.step: Centroid of $XYZ$ is the same point
